page_summary:
The Simulacra is the canonical works record for PKD's novel. It preserves a single archive manifestation and gives the work a stable bibliographic home. The preserved item here is The Simulacra (1964). The archive copy runs 222 pages.

Researchers can use this entry to trace publication context, later commentary, and relationships to other works.

structure.form: novel with a large ensemble cast whose separate plotlines converge around the central deception of Nicole Thibodeaux's manufactured, ageless public persona

characters.name: Nicole Thibodeaux
characters.note: An eternally youthful, beloved public persona maintained across decades through institutional stage management rather than a single continuous human life -- the novel's central object of both public devotion and hidden manipulation.

characters.name: Various USEA functionaries
characters.note: Maintain and gradually threaten to expose the mechanism behind Nicole's manufactured persona and the android nature of 'der Alte,' the rotating presidential figurehead.

settings.name: The USEA (United States of Europe and America)
settings.note: A merged transatlantic political entity whose actual governance depends on a manufactured, endlessly renewed public symbol rather than any transparent democratic process.

motifs: A beloved public figure maintained as an ageless media construct, with the machinery behind the illusion hidden from the population that adores her
Political legitimacy manufactured through stagecraft and propaganda rather than genuine continuous rule
The outlawing of independent psychological treatment in favor of state-controlled therapeutic technology
Competing institutional interests in whether to preserve or expose a foundational public deception, weighed against social stability
reading.significance: The Simulacra is one of Dick's most direct satires of manufactured political celebrity and mass-media governance, anticipating later cultural anxieties about deepfakes, stage-managed public figures, and manufactured political continuity by decades. Nicole Thibodeaux is widely read as a composite critique of Jacqueline Kennedy-style political celebrity and the cult of personality more broadly, her ageless persona standing in for the way media apparatuses can sustain a beloved public fiction indefinitely regardless of the reality behind it. The novel's dense ensemble structure -- typical of Dick's mid-1960s novels -- lets the central deception be viewed from multiple social positions simultaneously, from ordinary citizens who need the illusion to functionaries who manufacture it.
reading.closing_note: The novel's suggestion that the public's need for a stable, beloved symbolic figure may outlast any scandal capable of exposing the deception behind her offers one of Dick's bleaker verdicts on the durability of manufactured political belief.
